quote: I will bring them back to their own land.
firstReading: God promises to restore and gather Israel. In this passage the Lord declares that he will bring the people back from exile, turn their mourning into joy, and increase their numbers. Families are reunited as God leads them home; the hungry will be satisfied and their shame removed. The Lord’s steadfast love and power will ransom and redeem the remnant, reversing exile into a renewed flourishing and praise among the nations.
psalmSummary: The psalm summons the nations to hear and proclaims that the LORD will redeem Jacob and gather the exiles. It celebrates God’s deliverance: the people are ransomed, restored, and transformed from sorrow into gladness. Young women and children express renewed joy; the community offers thanksgiving and praise for the Lord’s saving action and faithful care in bringing the scattered home.
gospelSummary: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon and encounters a Canaanite woman pleading for her demon-possessed daughter. At first Jesus gives no answer and his disciples urge him to send her away. When he says he was sent only to Israel, she humbly persists, kneeling and acknowledging even dogs eat crumbs from their masters’ table. Jesus praises her faith and grants her request; her daughter is healed. The episode highlights persistent faith, unexpected receptivity to a Gentile, and the widening of God’s mercy beyond Israel.
saintReflection: No saint is listed for today, but the readings invite reflection on a saintly quality: persistent, humble faith. Like the Canaanite woman, the faithful recognize their need, do not claim entitlement, and persevere in pleading for mercy. Jeremiah’s promise of return likewise shows God’s faithfulness to those who rely on him; Christians are called to trust God’s power to restore and to intercede confidently for others.
dailyPrayer: Merciful God, your loving hand gathers your scattered people and turns mourning into joy. Give us the humility and perseverance of the Canaanite woman who knelt before Jesus and trusted in your mercy. Help us to plead for those in need with unshaken faith, to welcome outsiders as heirs of your promise, and to work for the restoration of broken families and communities. Open our hearts to the breadth of your compassion so that your Church becomes a sign of reconciliation. Fill us with praise and thanksgiving for your saving deeds, and teach us to trust you for healing and new life. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis: Jeremiah’s promise of return and the psalm’s song of ransom frame God as the restorer of a broken people; the power of divine fidelity reverses exile into praise. The Gospel scene places that promise alongside a concrete encounter in which Jesus’ mercy overflows ethnic boundaries. The woman’s humble persistence models a faith that attains healing when Israel’s mission is expanded to include Gentiles. Together these texts emphasize covenant continuity: God remains faithful to Israel’s restoration while revealing a universal mercy that invites all peoples. The readings prompt the Church to embody persistent intercession, welcome, and restorative justice as signs of God’s kingdom.
exegesis:
Context: Jeremiah 31:1–7 comes from a larger prophetic assurance that follows darker oracles: after warnings of judgment, the prophet moves to a voice of hope. Historically the address sits amid the trauma of exile and the longing for return. Jeremiah’s rhetoric deliberately uses familial and covenantal language—"I will bring them back," images of gathering, and promises of increase—to portray God as both judge and restorer. The restoration is not merely territorial but social and spiritual: families are reunited, shame is removed, and God’s steadfast love is the motivating power for renewal.

Psalm: The selected psalm verses echo Jeremiah’s theme, calling nations to hear and celebrating the LORD’s redeeming action. The psalmist frames restoration as both divine initiative and communal rejoicing: the Lord ransoms Jacob and brings Israel home, and the response is thanksgiving, dancing, and new life for women and children. Liturgically the psalm functions to translate prophetic hope into worship, turning the historical promise into present praise. It accentuates the communal and generational dimensions of redemption—the whole body of Israel experiences reversal of fortune.

Gospel: Matthew 15:21–28 narrates a striking encounter in Gentile territory. Jesus’ initial silence and the disciples’ rebuke create narrative tension, and Jesus’ remark about being sent to Israel sets the stage for a theological test. The woman’s repartee—acknowledging her outsider status yet asserting that dogs eat the crumbs—demonstrates insight, humility, and bold faith. Jesus’ commendation, "Woman, great is your faith," is the climax: faith, not ethnic identity, becomes the decisive category for receiving mercy. The episode thus reveals the expansion of God’s saving action and Jesus’ openness to unexpected recipients of grace.

Saints: Although no named saint is appointed today, the Canaanite woman functions as a model saintly figure: persistent, humble, and theologically acute. Her stance embodies the virtues celebrated in Jeremiah and the psalm—trust in God’s power to redeem and a heart turned toward God even from the margins. The Church’s tradition often reads such figures as precursors of Gentile inclusion, and they invite believers to emulate a prayerful insistence in petitions, a willingness to kneel, and a readiness to accept mercy without presumption.

Exegetical notes: Several literary moves are instructive. Jeremiah’s repeated future-tense verbs and familial metaphors create a concrete promise that counters exile’s dislocation. The psalm’s summons to nations indicates that Israel’s restoration has a prophetic, even missionary, horizon. In Matthew the literary irony of Jesus’ apparent rebuke becomes a pedagogical device: the woman’s reply turns Jesus’ words inside out, teaching both disciples and readers about faith’s true locus. Theologically, the interplay of prophetic promise and Gospel narrative shows continuity: God’s covenant fidelity to Israel is the gateway to a broader economy of salvation.

Today: For contemporary readers the texts press pastoral and ecclesial questions. How does the Church enact restorative practices that heal exile—social, familial, spiritual? How are outsiders welcomed and their faith recognized? The Canaanite woman’s example challenges complacency: mercy often comes when the faithful persist without entitlement. Jeremiah’s hope and the psalm’s song invite communities to ground mission in thanksgiving and to trust that God can transform sorrow into praise. Practically, these readings inspire ministries of reconciliation, persistent prayer, and efforts to remove barriers to God’s mercy in our communities.
